correctness.rationale: Exhaustiveness is proved by a bijection between de Bruijn cycles rooted at the unique 00000 state and 32-cycle permutations induced by 16-bit truth tables. The finite loop considers all 65,536 tables, and a separately parametrized DFS enumerator yields exactly the same set of 2,048 rooted words. Direct signed cyclic dot products and independently rotated bitset XOR counts agree for every nonzero shift of every word. Exact table assertions include all 20 positive cells, the other ten zero cells, margins and known independent controls. The verifier ran and returned VERIFY_OK. Scope is strictly finite order five.

originality.rationale: The claim is the complete simultaneous (minimum negative, maximum positive) out-of-phase periodic-autocorrelation distribution of all 2,048 binary order-five de Bruijn cycles. Spinsante et al. (2011) give the 12- and 784-member absolute-peak subfamilies, and Fujisaki–Nabeshima (2011) report extremal and runner-up separate sidelobes at this order. Those prior results are recovered as strict aggregate controls but do not imply the joint table. The inspected full primary materials contain no complete contingency distribution; focused semantic and bibliographic searches yielded no exact equivalent. This is qualified scientific originality, not independent priority certification.
residual_risks: An unindexed or inaccessible earlier computational table could independently give the same full joint distribution.

value.rationale: Two 2011 studies explicitly motivate sequence selection by periodic autocorrelation, while their published extremal levels and small absolute-threshold subfamilies leave the full two-sided distribution unknown from those statements. The natural joint invariant answers every simultaneous low-negative/low-positive sidelobe constraint at the first nontrivial 2,048-cycle benchmark, determines the feasible range of pair types, and identifies four cycles with no positive offpeak correlation. It is a complete exact distribution, not just a slight improvement in a known bound or an arbitrary unmotivated slice.
